newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Matahari upbeat on 97 outlook.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Matahari upbeat on 97 outlook.

text.p: Indonesian retailer PT Matahari Putra Prima said on Monday it was confident it would reach its net profit target of 91 billion rupiah this year.

"If we we look at the industry itself, there is no reason why we cannot be upbeat," Matahari finance director Hanifah Komala told a news conference after a shareholders' meeting. "This year we will open of seven more outlets, but I can't give you details on the investment yet."

Matahari said it had won shareholder approval to pay a 1996 dividend of 15 rupiah per share and split the nominal value of its stock. The counter closed at 4,450 rupiah, a gain of 125 rupiah, with 461,00 shares changing hands.

Matahari also said it posted a net profit of 41.3 billion rupiah in the first quarter, sharply higher than the 21.8 billion rupiah in the same period last year. The company has set a net profit target of 91 billion rupiah for 1997, 121 billion rupiah for 1998 and 166 billion rupiah for 1999.
It posted net profit of 15.1 billion rupiah in 1996 on sales of 1.9 trillion rupiah.

"We are on target to reach 91 billion rupiah in net profit this year. We have also noticed that sales started to pick up in June. In general, our (annual) sales growth ranges between 10 and 12 percent," Komala said without giving other details.

Matahari's president Hari Darmawan earlier told the shareholders meeting the decision to split the nominal value of the stock to 500 rupiah from the current 1,000 rupiah was designed at boosting liquidity.
"The management believes that this is the best time to split the stock," Darmawan said.
Komala said Matahari, which currently has 82 outlets throughout the country, also planned to open between eight and 10 outlets in 1998.

He said the company did not see any impact from a government order barring retail chains from opening new stores in towns below the level of provincial capitals in a bid to promote small and medium traders.
"I don't see any impact on Matahari. We will support the government policy and we believe the policy is reasonable," he added.
Komala said he believed the regulation would not affect sales at all. "We already have at least 33 outlets (at levels below provincial capitals)," he said.
Analysts say large retailers accounted for 85 percent of total sales in 1995. Indonesia's large retailers include Matahari, Ramayana and Hero Supermarket.
Komala also said the company was ready to participate in the government's decree that existing retail chains in regional towns establish partnerships with small and medium retailers.
The government has said partnerships could be either sub-contracting arrangements for consignments or rental space in department stores and modern shopping centres for small firms.
